speechtext: On May 27 the hon member for Antigonish-GuySborough (Mr. Duff) moved for the production of papers. These papers subject to the limitation which I then expressed, are now presented. A number of the dispatches are of a confidential character,
On the order for the introduction by Mr. Reid of a bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act:

I will now give a decision on the motion of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) for leave to introduce a bill. When the hon. member for New Westminster moved on Thursday last for leave to introduce the bill standing on the order paper in his name-an act to amend the Bank of Canada Act-he stated in part, as Deported at page 3338 of Hansard, that "There are two changes contemplated in the proposed bill; the first is to amend paragraph (lb), subsection 3 of section 25, and would empower the minister to purchase silver for the redemption of dominion notes."
If it is true that the bill will do what its sponsor states, empower the minister to purchase silver, then it will be generally agreed that it is out of order on the ground that a private member cannot introduce a measure which involves the expenditure of public moneys.
Upon looking up original section 25, I find that paragraph (b) of subsection 3 of the Bank of Canada Act, reads as follows:
3.	On the day on which the bank is authorized to commence business the minister shall transfer to the bank-
(b) silver held by the minister for the redemption of dominion notes valued at the market price of the fine silver content thereof.
Bank oj Canada

Mr. Reid's amendment proposes to add to subsection (b) just referred to the following words:
and at any time thereafter the minister may transfer to the bank silver held by him for the redemption of dominion notes or hereafter purchased for the redemption of dominion notes valued at the market price of the fine silver content.
The original section as just quoted provides that "on the day on which the bank is authorized to commence business, the minister shall transfer to the bank silver held by him for the redemption of dominion notes." The amendment provides that "any time thereafter the minister may transfer to the bank silver held by him for the redemption of dominion notes or hereafter purchased for the redemption of dominion notes," etcetera.
While I do not think the amendment goes as far as the hon. member suggests, that is "empowers" the minister to purchase silver, it certainly -contemplates the purchase of further silver by the minister and does empower the transfer of silver held by him to the bank.
The purchase of silver by the government certainly involves the expenditures of government moneys. Speaking of silver in the narrow sense as " money," its transfer from the minister to the bank, as authorized by the proposed amendment, involves the expenditure of public moneys. It is quite clear that legislation involving the expenditure of public moneys can only be introduced by a responsible minister of the crown upon the recommendation of His Excellency the Governor General. On the ground that the expenditure of public moneys is involved the amending motion is out of order.
It is, in my opinion, also out of order on a second ground. Giving silver the wider meaning of "property" its transfer as proposed by the amendment involves the disposal or alienation of crown property. No private member may introduce a measure for this purpose without first having asked the house to agree to an address for leave to proceed thereon, such leave to be obtained prior to the introduction of the bill. (See Bourinot 4th edition, page 414.) No such leave has been obtained.
I therefore rule that the motion to introduce the bill in question is out of order.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the thought and the great care you have given the matter, and also the fairness with which you have dealt with it. But I must say I am disappointed at being prohibited from introducing this bill.

maintopic: TRAIL, B.C., SMELTER APPROVAL OF CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES CONCERNING DAMAGE COMPLAINED OF IN THE STATE OF WASHINGTON

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRAIL, B.C., SMELTER APPROVAL OF CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES CONCERNING DAMAGE COMPLAINED OF IN THE STATE OF WASHINGTON
speechtext:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the following convention between Canada and the United States: relating to certain complaints arising from the operation of the smelter at Trail, British Columbia, signed at Ottawa on the 15th day of April, 1935. Convention Between Canada and the United States
Relating to Certain Complaints Arising from the Operation of the Smelter at Trail, BjC.
Ottawa, April 15, 1935. His Majesty the King of Great Britain. Ireland and the British dominions beyond the Seas, Emperor of India, in respect of the Dominion of Canada, and The President of the United States of America.
Consider i ng that the government of the United States has complained to the government of Canada that fumes discharged from the smelter of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company at Trail, British 'Columbia, have been causing damage in the state of Washington, and	.
Considering further that the international joint commission, established pursuant to the Boundary Waters treaty of 1909, investigated problems arising from the operation of the smelter at Trail and rendered a report and recommendations thereon, dated February 28, 1931, and
Recognizing the desirability and necessity of effecting a permanent settlement,
Have decided to conclude a convention for the purposes aforesaid, and to that end have named as their respective plenipotentiaries:
His Majesty the King of Great Britain, Ireland and the British dominions beyond the Seas, Emperor of India, for the Dominion of Canada:
The Right Honourable Richard Bedford Bennett, Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Secretary of State for External Affairs;
The President of the United States of America:
Pierre de L. Boal. Charge d'Affaires ad interim of the United States of America at Ottawa;
Who, after having communicated to each other their full powers, found in good and due form, have agreed upon the following articles:
Article I
The government of Canada will cause to be paid to the secretary of state of the United States, to be deposited in the United States treasury, within three months .after ratifications of this convention have been exchanged, the sum of three hundred and fifty thousand dollars, United States currency, in payment of all damage which occurred in the United States, prior to the first day of January, 1932, as a result of the operation of the Trail smelter.
Article II
The governments of Canada and the United States, hereinafter referred to as "the governments," mutually agree to constitute a tribunal hereinafter referred to as "the tribunal," for the purpose of deciding the questions referred to it under the provisions of article III. The tribunal shall consist of a chairman and two national members.
The chairman shall be a jurist of repute who is neither a British subject .nor a citizen of the United States. Ho shall be chosen by the governments', or, in the event of failure to reach agreement within nine months after the exchange of ratifications of this convention, by the president of the permanent administrative council of the permanent court of arbitration at The Hague described in -article 49 of the convention for the pacific settlement of international disputes concluded at The Hague on October 18, 1007.
The two national members shall be jurists of repute, who have not been associated directly or indirectly, in the present controversy. One member shall be chosen by each of the governments.
The governments miay each designate a scientist to assist the tribunal.
Article III
The tribunal shall finally decide the questions. hereinafter referred to as " the questions," set forth hereunder, namely:-
(1)	Whether damage caused by the Trail smelter in the state of Washington has occurred since the first day of January, 1932, and, if so, what indemnity should be paid therefor?
(2)	In the event of the answer to the first part of the preceding question being in the affirmative, whether the Trail smelter should
Trail Smelter

be required to refrain from causing damage in the state of Washington in the future and, if so, to what extent?
(3)	In the light of the answer to the preceding question, what measures or regime, if any, should be adopted or maintained by the Trail smelter ?
(4)	What indemnity or compensation, if any, should be paid on account of any decision or decisions rendered by the tribunal pursuant to the next two preceding questions?
Article IV
The tribunal shall apply the law and practice followed in dealing with cognate questions in the United States of America as well as international law and practice, and shall give consideration to the desire of the high contracting parties to reach a solution just to all parties concerned.
Article V
The procedure in this adjudication shall be as follows:

1.	Within nine months from the date of the exchange of ratifications of this agreement, the agent for the government of the United States shall present to the agent for the government of Canada a statement of the facts, together with the supporting evidence, on which the government of the United States rests its complaint and petition.
2.	Within a like period of nine months from the date on which this agreement becomes effective, as aforesaid, the agent for the government of Canada shall present to the agent for the government of the United States a statement of the facts, together with the supporting evidence, relied upon by the government of Canada.
3.	Within six months from the date on which the exchange of statements and evidence provided for in paragraphs 1 and 2 of this article has been completed, each agent shall present in the manner prescribed by paragraphs 1 and 2 an answer to the statement of the other with any additional evidence and such argument as he may desire to submit.
Article VI
When the development of the record is completed in accordance with article V hereof the governments shall forthwith cause to be forwarded to each member of the tribunal a complete set of the statements, answers, evidence and arguments presented by their respective agents to each other.
Article VII
After the delivery of the record to the members of the tribunal in accordance with article VI the tribunal shall convene at a time and place to be agreed upon by the two governments for the purpose of deciding upon such further procedure as it may be deemed necessary to take. In determining upon such further procedure and arranging subsequent meetings, the tribunal will consider the individual or joint requests of the agents of the two governments.
Article VIII
The tribunal shall hear such representations and shall receive and consider such evidence, oral or documentary, as may be presented by

the governments or by interested parties, and for that purpose shall have power to administer oatihs. The tribunal shall have authority to make such investigations as it may deem necessary and expedient, consistent with other provisions of this convention.
Article IX
The chairman shall preside at all hearings and other meetings of the tribunal, and shall rule upon all questions of evidence and procedure. In reaching a final determination of each or any of the questions, the chairman and the two members shall each have one vote, and, in the event of difference, the opinion of the majority shall prevail, and the dissent of the chairman or member, as the case may be, shall be recorded. In the event that no two members of the tribunal agree on a question, the chairman shall make the decision.
Article X
The tribunal, in determining the first question and in deciding upon the indemnity, if any, which should be paid in respect to the years 1932 and 1933, shall give due regard to the results of investigations and inquiries made in subsequent years.
Investigators, whether appointed by or on behalf of the governments, either jointly or severally, or the tribunal, shall be permitted at all reasonable times to enter and view and carry on investigations upon any of the properties upon which damage is claimed to have occurred or to be occurring, and their reports may, either jointly or severally, be submitted to and received by the tribunal for the purpose of enabling the tribunal to decide upon any of the questions.
Article XI
The tribunal shall report to toe governments its final decisions, together with toe reasons on which they are based, as soon as it has reached its conclusions in respect to the questions, and within a period of three months after the conclusion of proceedings. Proceedings shall be deemed to have been concluded when the agents of the two governments jointly inform the tribunal that they have nothing additional to present. Such period may be extended by agreement of the two governments.
Upon receiving such report, toe governments may make arrangements for toe disposition of claims for indemnity for damage, if any, which may occur subsequently to toe period of time covered by such report.
Article XII
The governments undertake to take such action as may be necessary in order to ensure due performance of the obligations undertaken hereunder, in compliance with toe decision of the tribunal.
Article XIII
Each government shall pay the expenses of toe presentation and conduct of its case before toe tribunal and toe expenses of its national member and scientific assistant.
All other expenses, which by their nature are a charge on both governments, including toe honorarium of toe neutral member of toe tribunal, shall be borne by the two governments in. equal moieties.

Trail Smelter
Article XIV
This agreement shall be ratified in accordance with the constitutional forms of the contracting parties and shall take effect immediately upon the exchange of ratifications, which shall take place at Ottawa as soon as possible.
In witness whereof, the respective plenipotentiaries have signed this convention and have hereunto affixed their seals.
Done in duplicate at Ottawa this fifteenth day of April, in the year of our Lord, one thousand, nine hundred and thirty-five.
(L.S.) R. B. Bennett.

And that this house do approve of the same
He said: Mr. Speaker, the convention which this house is asked to ratify deals with an agreement arrived at between the governments of the United States and Canada with respect to a matter that has been the subject of controversy for many years. When this government came into office in August, 1930, the subject matter of the dispute had been under consideration by the international joint commission who made a report in 1931, in which they recommended that $350,000 should be paid the farmers and others in the state of Washington who had suffered under the circumstances to which I shall presently refer.
As is well known the smelter at Trail is near the boundary line between Canada and the United States. In the course of its operations the chimneys emit large quantities of smoke which is heavily laden with poisonous substances that affect vegetation very adversely. Those members of this house who have visited one of the islands off the Pacific coast will recall that as they approached the harbour they observed that the vegetation had been entirely destroyed by the fumes from the smelter at that point. Prevailing winds carried the gases emitted from the chimneys of the smelter into the United States, and of course they had the effect of seriously injuring the vegetation of that area over which they circulated. The grasses, grains, flowers and to some extent the trees Were greatly injured by these fumes and the farmers of the United States, through their government, claimed that the loss was substantial.
An agreement was arrived at between the two governments, the government of Canada and the government of the United States, by which the international joint commission investigated the matter as I have indicated, but those findings were not final; the commission acted only in an advisory capacity and not for the purpose of rendering a final judgment. The sum of $250,000 was recommended to be paid; the finding in that regard was unanimous, but the citizens of the locality affected in the state of Washington complained
that this was not adequate and that the principles upon which the international joint commission had proceeded did not fully take into consideration the circumstances in connection with the injuries sustained. Much discussion has taken place; finally this convention has been arrived at. The $350,000 is to be taken on account, so to speak, up to the date indicated by the convention. That money, of course, is not provided by the Dominion of Canada; it is provided by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company and has been made available to the government of Canada for payment to the United States.
The provisions of the convention to which particular attention should be directed are found in articles II and III. In article II it will be observed that a tribunal is to be constituted, to consist of a chairman and two national members. The article continues:
The chairman shall be a jurist of repute who is neither a British subject nor a citizen of the United States. He shall be chosen by the governments, or, in the event of failure to reach agreement within nine months after the exchange of ratifications of this convention, by the president of the permanent administrative council of the permanent court of arbitration at The Hague described in article 49 of the convention for the pacific settlement of international disputes concluded at The Hague on October 18, 1907.
The two national members shall be jurists of repute, who have not been associated directly or indirectly, in the present controversy. One member shall be chosen by each of the governments.
What they are to determine is set out in the questions mentioned in article III, as follows:
(1)	Whether damage caused by the Trail smelter in the state of Washington has occurred since the first day of January, 1932. and', if so, what indemnity should be paid therefor ?
(2)	In the event of the answer to the first part of the preceding question being in the affirmative, whether the Trail smelter should be required to refrain from causing damage in the state of Washington in the future and, if so, what extent?
(3)	In the light of the answer to the preceding question, what measures or regime, if any. should be adopted or maintained by the Trail smelter?
(4)	What indemnity or compensation, if any, should he paid on account of any decision or decisions rendered by the tribunal pursuant to the next two preceding questions?
I think perhaps the house is not concerned at the moment except with respect to the two articles I have mentioned; that is, the circumstances under which the tribunal is coming into being, the personnel of the tribunal and the questions to be determined. I need hardly say to the house that the finan-
Trail Smelter

cial obligations under which this country may be placed by reason of any determination of this tribunal will foe paid by the smelter company affected under an arrangement that has been made with them.
The question as to why the Dominion of Canada should be in the matter at all received very careful consideration before this government came into office, and it was felt that the only method by which the claim made by nationals of our neighbour could be disposed of satisfactorily would be through some action taken by the national government of this country on the one hand and of the United States on the other. When the international joint commission reported up to the end of 1931, the matter now is being treated as having been concluded up to that point, and the payment of money is being made for the liabilities that resulted from the poisonous fumes circulating in the state of Washington up to the date of that award.
I do not think there are any other questions calling for consideration in connection with this convention. If there are I shall be very glad to endeavour to answer them. I may add that the convention has been ratified by the senate of the United States.

PURCHASE, STORAGE AND MARKETING OP WHEAT .	AND OTHER GRAINS
Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to establish a board to be known as the Canadian grain board with power to purchase, receive and take delivery of wheat, oats, barley, rye and flax-seed, or any one or more of such grains for marketing and to sell, store, transport and market such grains, and to provide for the appointment of such clerks, employees and assistance as may be necessary, and to provide for their remuneration and for the expenses of, and arising out of, the operations of the board.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to make a lengthy speech to-day upon this matter, or at any rate at this stage, because obviously what I might say would probably be in response to questions which might be asked, and it is perfectly clear that there is no opportunity to do that in the mere movement of the house into committee to consider the resolution.

Grain Board-Mr. Bennett
I think possibly I should say that once in this country we had a grain board brought about, of course, by the exigencies of the war. The situation at the present time, without going into the matter in detail, is that this country has not been able to market all its wheat, and that there is a large surplus of unsold wheat, or an accumulation of surpluses beginning in 1929 and followed by a further large carryover in 1930 and in succeeding years, by reason of large crops.
I shall not at the moment deal with the political side of the observations which have been, made by hon. gentlemen opposite, because the matter is far too serious to discuss from the standpoint of narrow party politics. I should like to say however that I am prepared to give the committee the fullest information as to the world movement of wheat to indicate, notwithstanding what has been said notably by the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) that tariffs had something to do in preventing the sale of wheat in France and Germany. If the hon. member would just look at the imports into France, the imports into Germany and the imports into Italy I think he would probably arrive at a different conclusion.. AH that is necessary to do is to point out that there has been no diminution in the use of wheat by the people of the world and that, for instance in 1934 the entire wheat purchases by France were from Canada, with the exception of 1,000,000 bushels. All the wheat France imported from abroad, with the exception of something like 1,000,000 bushels, came from Canada, and that of the importations into Germany the greater part came from Canada. But those importations were very trifling. For instance, in the last five years the largest sale of wheat to France was 31,000,000 bushels. That was a period of time, of course, when France was not herself producing ample wheat for her own requirements.
I have already traversed this matter on more than one occasion, and to-day I desire only to make this simple observation, that owing to the result of post-war action on the part of countries which -were formerly wheat importing countries they have placed themselves in a position where to a very large extent they are free from the necessity of importing wheat from any country. For instance today France is a large exporter of wheat. In the year 1934 she exported large quantities of both wheat and flour to Great Britain and to other parts of the world. I suppose it must be known to hon. members that in this present year France is exporting wheat,-denatured wheat,-to the United States under the world's
wheat agreement. I might add that the Pontine imarshes of Italy, now available for the production of wheat, has placed under cultivation thousands of acres which never before produced wheat, and the use of fertilizers has increased the yield per acre in Germany to an extent even greater than it was before the war.
The essential fact for us to recall is that the countries of Europe which during the war did not produce wheat found themselves dependent upon the countries which did increase their production, notably Canada, and that unfortunately for us for some strange reason we did not realize that in 1925, 1926, 1927, 1928, 1929 and 1930 the countries of Europe had recovered their pre-war position-not only recovered it, but greatly strengthened it, and were' supplying not only their own requirements but were also on an export basis.
Under these circumstances the position was a very simple one. The question was whether or not chaos should reign in respect to the largest industry we have, in point of value of exports, or whether something should be done to endeavour to save it from the chaotic condition prevailing. Something was done. It may be that there is some desire to discuss the matter at length. I am prepared to do it in every detail and in every particular. It will be recalled that when before a committee opportunity was afforded for discussing the matter in detail, by a majority vote it was decided that such discussion would not be in the public interest. The determining factor at that time in the committee was hon. gentlemen opposite.
But eliminating that consideration for the moment I am merely pointing out that the world has been producing so much more wheat than it has been consuming that there is a large surplus, and that that surplus must be taken care of by some orderly method or we will have a complete dislocation of the whole wheat industry in Canada. We might as well face it frankly. I am not going to dwell upon these matters at this time further than to say that there were certain well defined conditions which during war time necessitated the creation of a wheat board. At the present time we have a condition whereby we have large quantities of wheat unsold. We and the rest of the world, namely the wheat producing countries of the world, have a substantial surplus of wheat over world requirements, but, as I have stated previously I shall not go into a detailed discussion. of the matter at this time. I merely state that I am in a position to give the figures when they are required.

Grain Board-Mr. Mackenzie King
I desire to direct the attention of the house to the particulars of the resolution itself. Assuming that the house is of the opinion that it is desirable in the public interest that there should1 be a board to deal with the most extraordinary situation that has ever existed in regard to wheat so far as we have a record, because it will be recalled that the price of wheat in 1932-33 reached the lowest point in four hundred years-there is a complete record of the price of wheat in the various parts of the world for over four hundred years, and as I say wheat never reached a lower price in five hundred years than it did in 1932-33"-under those circumstances, and with the surplus now existing it becomes essential to deal with the situation in some orderly manner. To the extent to which it may be possible to do so except through a wheat board I shall be very glad indeed to hear opinions expressed by members of this house. But if we conclude, as I believe the house will, that a wheat board is essential, then you ask yourself two simple questions: First, what power has this parliament to create such a board; and second, what shall be its powers?
With respect to the first, there has been a modification of the legal position by reason of the fact that the Grain Act was amended when it was decided by the supreme court, by a majority with the Chief Justice dissenting, that the Grain Act was ultra vires in so far as certain sections of it were concerned; and it was indicated that it could be made intra vires if the facilities or elevators were declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada. And so. under section 233 of the Grain Act, as consolidated in 1927, the declaration is made that these elevators, which are usually on the right of way of various railway companies, are works for the general' advantages of Canada.
The bill predicated1 upon this resolution would limit its operation to interprovincial and international trade. It would not seek to deal with purely domestic trade in any one province for that might be entirely beyond our jurisdiction.
The next question is, what shall be the powers of the board1? The board will1 be empowered, as the resolution indicates, to deal with wheat as buyers and sellers and the sole marketers of it for the purpose of ensuring that it shall find at least as large a market as possible under the circumstances that now exist.
That is all that can be usefully said1 on the resolution itself, but at the appropriate time I shall make a more extensive statement than that which I have now made.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR

I should like the minister to give the committee some explanation of this bill. We have already upon the statute books a law concerning the hours of labour on public works and under public contracts. I can see that this bill is to add the forty-four hour week to the eight hour day which exists under the present law. But this is going to apply to public works. I wonder whether it is worth while to enact this legislation at this time when this country has delegates sitting even to-day at Geneva for the purpose of considering a draft convention to establish a forty hour week, more particularly on public works either undertaken by governments or subsidized by them. The international labour conference which is now sitting and where we are represented is at this moment studying this very question, except that instead of a forty-four hour week as proposed by this legislation, the draft convention contemplates a forty-hour week on public works either undertaken by the governments themselves or subsidized by them. I would like my hon. friend to tell the committee w'hat is the stand of Canada on the draft convention which is being submitted at Geneva at the present time. It seems that by asking the house to enact this legislation, the government is not favouring the draft convention which is being submitted to our delegates at Geneva.

Fair Wages and Hours oj Labour
I should also like my hon. friend to say whether the delegates of the ' government of Canada have special instructions as to the stand they are to [DOT] take on this Geneva convention.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill
is obvious. We have now an enactment respecting fair wages and an eight hour day for labour employed on public works for the Dominion of Canada. The substantial changes* in the present bill are to implement the royal commission's report by way of the adoption of a forty-four hour week with respect, to contracts for the construction, repair and so forth of federal buildings and the adoption of an eight hour day in connection with work that may be performed by a province or any other body to which the dominion government subscribes public money.
The reason is not obscure why a forty-four hour week is not imposed under section 5. It was thought by the law officers of the crown and those who advised in the preparation of the legislation that the adoption of a forty-four hour week with respect to the class of work contemplated by section 5 might very well give rise to an invitation to impeach the validity of the legislation on the ground of its unconstitutionality. Those are the substantial changes that are .made in the bill from the provisions which prevail in the enactment now on the statute books.
With regard to the deliberations now being carried on at Geneva with respect to a forty hour week on similar works, I would say only this: if such a convention is adopted at Geneva, is ultimately ratified here in Canada and is translated into legislative enactment, then it will be, I think, soon enough for us to take a further progressive step in the reduction of hours of labour. These things cannot all come at once. I would prefer- and I say this with the greatest respect to the hon. member for Quebec East-to take these matters up in progressive steps as we are sure of our course and certain of the legality of the legislation which we are enacting.

speechtext:
As the hon. member knows, communications between Geneva and the government of Canada are carried on through the Department of External Affairs. The Department of Labour was advised of this discussion. I think the hon. member in 92582-2204
this and other matters has overlooked the fact that no draft convention binds any country until such time as that country accedes to it. It is for the parliament of Canada to say whether or not it accedes to it. If it is unanimous on this as it has been on other conventions submitted to it during the present session, there should be no objection on that score. But- the government take the view, rightly or wrongly, that inasmuch as at this session of parliament we had expressed in formal terms our approval of the convention, our delegates should be instructed to inform the committee at Geneva of that fact and indicate that this government was not at the moment prepared to instruct its representatives to vote for or against the draft convention for a forty hour week but would rather they indicate what we were doing and state that if the draft convention were passed and recommended by the international labour office-it is not, as the hon. gentleman has said, the international labour conference-and the convention, if one were arrived at, dispatched to us as soon as possible we would communicate, as we have done heretofore, with the various provinces to indicate just what had taken place so that thej' might make their representations known to the parliament of Canada to enable it to determine what action it would take in the way of approving or disapproving the draft convention. But in view of the fact that this bill was standing on the order paper from the earlier part of the session we would not instruct our delegates to vote for or against such a draft convention but would ask them to indicate exactly what the position was and to act accordingly.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
I am grateful to my right hon. friend for stating that I had overlooked the fact we are not bound by this convention until we have ratified it. I knew that. I believe this parliament of Canada is not bound even when this draft convention is adopted over there. This question has been discussed previously. But I wish to draw my right hon. friend's attention to this fact. He seems to indicate that the delegates of Canada have no formal instruction to vote on this question when the draft convention is submitted to the conference. Well, that is what happened last year; in common with the delegates of other countries they abstained or refrained from voting, with the result that there was not a sufficient number of votes for the adoption of the draft convention. There was much criticism, in labour circles more particularly, with regard to the

Fair Wages and Hours of Labour
stand taken by the delegates of some of the governments at the conference. I infer from the statement of my right hon. friend that our delegates have no instructions even this year, and I am afraid that the result may be the same as last year.
However, I have no objection to this bill, except that it seems a little futile that we should enact this legislation at a time when the very matter of the length of the week of labour is being considered at an international conference where we are represented and our delegates are sitting.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
I think perhaps the hon. gentleman has overlooked the fact that even if a draft convention were arrived at there it might be five or six years before it would become effective. Therefore it is desirable that this legislation should be enacted in the meantime. Mere discussion at Geneva and arriving at a draft convention does not give it any validity as far as Canada or any country is concerned until it is ratified or acceded to. That is the reason they are called draft conventions. It may well take a period of years before final action is taken. But there is always ample opportunity to accede to the draft convention during the time that elapses from the time of its adoption by the international labour office and the time that it is sent forth to the world and a sufficient number of nations have indicated their approval to give it validity. The action taken at Geneva does not in any sense do more than launch the draft convention, to enable the nations to determine what action, they shall take. Canada's action at Geneva would not have any effect to bind Canada to a forty-hour week, that would have to be done by this parliament after the convention is settled and a sufficient number of nations have acceded to it to make it effective, as perhaps the hon. gentleman knows better than I, for he has followed these things longer and perhaps with more care. But I have satisfied myself that it is desirable to enact this legislation, having regard to the long period that may elapse before any substitute legislation may take its place.
As far as our own delegation is concerned, do I understand the hon. gentleman to recommend that our delegates should be empowered to vote for a convention containing a provision for a forty-hour week?

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: No, I should think the Canadian government should give instructions, whatever they foe, not place our delegates in a situation where they could refrain from taking a stand, as last year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: Last year there had been no ratification of the forty-four hour week, and it is because we have now taken that step that we have instructed our delegates to explain just what the facts are and that it is matter for discussion. The government has had no opportunity, in view of the ratification of the forty-eight hour week to discuss with the various provinces and bodies affected what might be their considered view with respect to this matter. But if as the hon. gentleman said, action is taken in the way of a draft convention, then this parliament will in the light of the knowledge it secures in the manner indicated be able to place before the Commons and the Senate a full statement with respect to the attitude of mind of those who may be affected.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: I failed to follow the argument of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) a- few minutes ago. I can understand that if after the ratification of a treaty we were bringing in legislation to implement that ratification it would be general legislation, and might have to be somewhat limited in character. But this bill does not provide general legislation w'th regard to the work day but is limited to the work day on public works, and works assisted by the government. I cannot quite see how the minister can take the ground that the dominion government is not competent to decide how long men may work on government works or contracts to which the dominion government is a party. It seems to me that in that case it is quite competent for this parliament to state any hours it pleases without in any way getting into constitutional difficulties.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
I do not think the question raised by the hon. member should cause any great difficulty. I am quite in agreement with him when he states that on purely federal works this parliament would have sovereign authority to make a one-hour week if it chose or a week of any other number of hours within the number contained in a week. The change with respect to purely federal works was to bring the construction of such works into harmony with the recommendations made by the royal commission on price spreads and mass buying. That amendment appears in section 3, subsection (1) (b) of the bill.
Then with respect to the new section, section 5, which deals with work to which the dominion, the federal state, may contribute by way of subsidy, loan, advance or guarantee; with respect to that class of work this enactment goes no further than the forty-eight hour week, because as I said a few

Fair Wages and. Hours of Labour
momenta ago, where the work is primarily-being carried1 on by another agency and the federal state merely contributes, then we might well imperil the legality of the bill by going further than we believe we have the right to go under the legislation recently introduced with respect to the adoption of the eight-hour day.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
That is the very
point.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Just a moment, I shall
try to clear this up. But while the legislation with respect to that class- of work confines the dominion to an eight-hour day ostensibly, yet-and I think this keeps us clearly within the law-there is nothing in my judgment to prevent this government entering into an agreement, say, with a province, say, with any other agency, where it seems proper that the federal state should subscribe, that one of the conditions of that agreement should be that it shall conform to a forty-four hour week or such other regulation as might be imported- into such an agreement as a condition for the advance.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: Then as I understand it would be quite competent for us in any section of this bill to provide for a forty-four hour week or a week of any number of hours?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: Forty-four is in.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
In one place it
says forty-eight. My suggestion is that it seems to be quite competent for us to provide in any section or all sections for the forty-four hour or even the forty h-our week.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: I am afraid I have not made myself clear. This parliament may insert any number of hours they want, and invite the impeachment of this law on constitutional grounds. That is what I do not want to see happen. But, as I have explained, in section 5-which deals with work to which the federal government may contribute-we are careful to see that we conform to the authorities and powers that we believe we presently have under the eight hour day bill which recently passed- through parliament.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
But surely we
would not need to contribute-

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
That is exactly what I
have explained. That matter can be easily made the subject of any agreement that may be entered into, and a condition imposed that certain hours of work will have to prevail if the contribution is to be made.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
With respect to the point under discussion, referring to government contracts that are entirely federal undertakings subsection (b) of section 3 says:
The working hours of persons while so employed shall not exceed eight hours per day nor forty-four hours per week-
Apparently the right to make that provision is unquestioned. Then turning to section 5, to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has referred, this deals with agreements for work involving dominion aid. That is, aid may -be granted by loan, by credit or by any other means, to any undertaking, and we must bear in mind that such aid always will be granted under some agreement with the province concerned. In any such agreement, according to this section, there shall be inserted certain stipulations, including:
-the following conditions respecting fair wages and hours of work, that is to say. the condition respecting fair wages set forth in paragraph (a) of subsection 1 of section 3 of this actand then-
-and the condition that the working hours of persons employed in the execution of the work shall not exceed eight hours per day-
The suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) is that there is no reason why there should not be inserted, after the eight hour provision, the phrase that appears in subsection (b) of section 3, "nor forty-four hours per week." I quite agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre; in fact I had made a notation to suggest that these words should be inserted.
With respect to the point raised by the Minister of Labour, as I followed him he indicated that this has not been put in because it might imperil the validity of the enactment. But if you read the section in question you will see that by this bill pro-vision is made setting a weekly maximum of forty-four hours in any undertaking into which a provincial or other body enters with the federal government, by inferring that in every agreement between this government and a province or municipality that provision will be inserted. But this whole section deals with cases in which aid is granted; this section sets out the agreement and then says that in every such agreement there shall be inserted certain stipulations. One is in connection with the eight hour day; another is in connection with the forty-four hour week. It seems to me that it is competent for this parliament to lay down the regulation that if the federal government enters into a contract with a province, a municipality or any other body

Fair Wages and Hours oj Labour
to grant aid, they can lay down the terms upon which that aid will be granted. So I submit that it would be quite competent for parliament to do so, and obviously it would be valid to insert those words in subsection 2 of section 5, namely the words "nor forty-four hours per week" after the words "eight hours per day," as appearing in subsection (b) of section 3, and I so suggest.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
I will only refer to the
point once again; at least I trust I will have to refer to it only once again. It is gratifying, at least, to note that two members from Winnipeg agree on one subject at the same time. In my mind there is a clear distinction in the interpretation of this section, and of course I get some comfort out of the thought that very eminent legal minds have assisted in drafting section 5. In this section it distinctly states that the working hours of persons employed in the execution of the work shall not exceed eight hours, per day. That is in harmony with the legislation which passed through this parliament only recently. Some hold the view that that legislation is not constitutional; the government believe it is constitutional. To avoid the possibility of an impeachment of this legislation by reason of an imposition, direct or implied, upon some other agency whether it be a province or a municipality-and the province is what I am directing my remarks to at the moment-the provision is made in the legislation itself that in the agreement which may be fashioned under the provisions of the bill the forty-eight hour week shall not be exceeded. I have no doubt, however, that operating under the bill itself and through to the agreement which may be entered into between this parliament or the executive as the case may be, and a province, it would be quite legal to bring the -working hours into harmony with the forty-four hour week or any lesser period of time that might be a condition imposed by this parliament when a grant was being made, and to withhold a grant under such an agreement if the spending authority did not conform to the condition that attached to the grant or guarantee.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
I do not know
whether or not we have made ourselves plain in this matter, but the legislation passed recently consonant with the ratification of the treaty was general legislation referring not merely to government contracts but to all work. It was in that connection that it was considered that if we had exceeded the terms of the treaty or the convention that legislation might have been regarded as unconstitutional. In this case, however, my point is that this bill deals particularly with IMr. D. M. Kennedy.]
dominion public works or such works as are assisted by dominion grants. That is a specific matter over which the dominion has control. In this measure we are discriminating between two classes of workers. On the one hand we have those on government contracts who are not permitted to work more than forty-hour hours a week; on the other hand w-e have those on contracts to which the dominion government makes grants, who are permitted to work forty-eight hours a week. The minister takes the ground that this section cannot be brought in harmony with the first section because we might invalidate the whole legislation.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: No. I say it can be done mder the agreement but not under the bill.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: I was going on to say that the minister says it can be arranged under the agreement, but if he will turn to subsection 2 of section 5 he will find the conditions to be stipulated in every such agreement. We are talking about the very thing to which he has referred. We ask that these conditions be stipulated in the agreement; we are not asking anything else. We are simply providing that this be put in black and white in the agreement. I cannot see how in connection with any agreement there could be any difficulty about inserting the provision for foi'ty-four hours, as was done in the preceding section.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
If I understand my hon. friend's objection correctly it is that the forty-four-hour provision should be stated in connection with all contracts made for work which is not strictly speaking work performed by government servants. We make contracts here, and we can stipulate in connection with our contracts the terms we expect to be carried out. But we also make grants to provinces and to municipalities in connection with works which they propose to carry out; those are grants in aid. As the bill was originally framed and submitted to council the clause applied to all works carried on in provinces and municipalities to which we had made government grants or appropriations.
The bill was then submitted to Mr. Tilley, K;C., and Mr. Geoffrion, K.C., and they both pointed out that that provision in regard to the work performed by contractors other than government contractors would be invalid and beyond the powers of this parliament, as contravening provincial legislative jurisdiction. But they both said, "You can achieve the purpose you have in view by inserting in your bill section 5, as it appears in this measure." Namely, it was indicated that we

Fair Wages and Hours oj Labour
could insert terms in our agreements with provinces and municipalities which would bind them in respect of any terms upon which we decided. They said that if we placed it in the bill it would constitute a clear infringement of provincial jurisdiction, but that we could put it in an agreement as a term or condition upon which a grant would be made, and that by doing that we would achieve the same end. Consequently the bill is in its present form.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: Subsection 2 contains the regulation with regard to an agreement, and it specifies that we shall enter into such agreements only under certain conditions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: To which subsection do you refer?

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: Subsection (2) of section 5. It reads "In every such agreement- "

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: "-there shall be inserted" the stipulations which I have mentioned.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: Yes, and we suggest that they be inserted in such a way as to ensure no more than eight hours a day or forty-four hours a week.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: We might wish to make them less than that.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: We are asking simply this, that subsection (2) be brought into conformity with section 3. I can see no objection to that. Of course, I hesitate to take issue with the eminent counsel to whom the minister has referred, but it does seem to me that we should not simply have great names hurled at us so as to silence us. We ought to use our own brains. The government has already sponsored certain legislation about which Mr. Tilley and the other eminent gentleman expressed some doubt.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: Some doubt is correct.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: There is no doubt expressed by them in connection with this matter.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
I should like to say a word on the point in question, namely, as to the validity of inserting after "eight hours per day" in subsection (2) of section 5 the words "nor forty-four hours per week."
I hesitate to differ from such eminent counsel as have been mentioned, but this subsection does not attempt to legislate as
to the hours which any province or municipality shall stipulate. It merely provides that if the federal government grants money in aid of a province or a municipality, or in fact any other body, then it shall insert certain provisions in the agreement. In the event of there being no such regulation, when the federal government came to deal with a province asking money in aid of works the federal authorities could work out an agreement. It would competent for the federal government to make such terms as they saw fit, so long as they agreed with the other bargaining party. They could agree that they would grant money only on the condition that the men working on the job worked a certain number of hours per week or day. This section proposes to give directions to the government when entering into any such agreement that they shall insert a provision that the workman shall not work more than eight hours per day. I submit it is perfectly competent for this parliament to instruct the government to insert in any such agreement a further provision that it shall not exceed forty-four hours per week. That would not be legislating for the provinces. It would simply place the federal government, when dealing with the provinces, in the position of deciding whether or not it will enter into an agreement to grant assistance in respect of works, and in the position of stating that they will grant assistance only when that provision appears in an agreement.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Fair wages.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
I believe section 2 has been copied from the present act and gives rise to some ambiguity. Unfortunately the draftsman has carried the phraseology into this seotion. The section begins with these words:
In this act, unless the context otherwise requires, "fair wages" means such wages _ as are generally accepted as current from time to time for competent workmen.
That wording, as hon. members will realize, might cause great confusion. A contract might be entered into to-day and wages change to-morrow. In order to clarify the situation I should like to move:
That section 2 of the bill be amended by striking out the words "from time to time" in the third line of the said section, and substituting therefor the words "at the date of the contract, when such work is being performed' by contract."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
I so move.

Fair Wages and Hours of Labour

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: May I ask the minister if that does not change the intention of the definition as set forth in the original act? Was the definition not intended to leave room for the possibility of altering the rate, assuming that the wages in the district were to alter over a period of time? For example, in a contract running for three or four years the rate might be one thing this year and another next year. I believe it was the intention in the original definition to indicate that if the general rate altered, the rate in the government contract should be made to correspond with it.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: I do not believe the amendment would clarify the situation. I am of the opinion the point raised by the right hon. gentleman is pertinent, and the difficulty he points out would cause trouble in the event of a contract continuing for twelve months. The whole clause appears to be ambiguous, because it uses the expression "accepted as current from time to time" or, as the amendment suggests, "at the date of the contract." I can find nothing in the section which in any way compels the government to accept any fair wage clause or fair wage legislation which may be in operation in the various provinces. There may be in operation in a province a fair wage act which specifies certain wages to be paid on a certain class of work to mechanics or labourers. Under its present wording this section does not indicate that the fair wage must be accepted. But there may be wages paid that are considerably below the wages specified in the fair wage act and yet it might be the current rate of pay. You might have a dual rate of pay in a district, and unless this clause is made more specific than it is at present it probably will give rise to a good deal of confusion and misunderstanding. I would like to see something in this clause which would compel the contractors in various parts of the country to accept wherever they are in effect the fair wage laws of the provinces and pay that rate of pay on all government contracts. I think the word "current" should be cut out entirely from the clause. At the present time I think the minister must know that there is a good deal of dissatisfaction, and strikes I believe in one or two places, where government contracts are being carried on because the wages paid are below even the accepted rates of pay as understood in those localities. If this clause is going to give rise to confusion I think the minister ought to make it more specific than it is at the present time in order that there may be no misunderstanding wherever government contracts happen to be let.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in the light of what the right hon. leader of the opposition has said we are prepared to drop the amendment. With respect to the observations made by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), if there has been any strike on federal government contracts by reason of the non-payment of fair wages I would like to be advised if the hon. member knows of any such strikes, because great care is taken and has always been taken by the Department of Labour to see that fa:r wages as defined by the act are inserted in the schedule attached to and which becomes a part of the agreement of every contractor who is contracting to do and is doing federal construction work. If that contractor does not pay the wages according to the schedule which is part of his contract, then when the Department of Labour is notified, and it does not need to be any formal notification, just a letter or a post card or a telegram, investigation is immediately made, and if it is found that in any class of labour on federal works the contractor as failing to pay the wages as stipulated by the Department of Labour and accepted by the Department of Public Works the amount is at once held back from the contractor until full investigation is made, and if it is found that the allegations are correct the amount is paid direct to those who have been underpaid according to the terms of the agreement.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
I will give the minister
privately a couple of instances perhaps later on in the afternoon, because I do not want to bring the names of any individuals into the discussion. But I do know of two instances. I think there is some trouble right now in the contract let for the building of a post office in Montreal. I have sent out for the newspaper files. There are also low wages being paid on government contracts in Manitoba, the facts of which I shall be glad to let the minister have.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: I would be glad to be advised of them.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
What I am trying to do, Mr. Chairman, is to have this clause made a little more specific than it is at the present time because the word "current" referring to current wages is very ambiguous. The wages in a district may be only thirty cents per hour, and yet the wage stipulated by the fair wage act of the province may be forty-five cents per hour. In that case the contractor would be quite justified, according to the wording of the act, in paying the lower rate of wages because strictly speaking he would be within the terms of the act. I am asking

Fair Wages and Hours oj Labour
the minister if he will not so word this clause as to compel the contractor to pay the wages as specified in the fair wage acts of the various provinces and of the dominion.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think that upon reflection the hon. member will not pursue that argument further. Surely the federal government is quite as able to determine what fair wages are as any province of Canada, and I do not say that disrespectfully of any province. If section 2 is examined further it will be observed that fair wages not only means "such wages as are generally accepted as current from time to time for competent workmen in the district in which the work is being performed," but at the end of the section there are these words, "but shall in all cases be such wages as are fair and reasonable." We have very .competent officials who determine both those sets of facts, if both have to be determined-what fair wages are generally accepted as current in the locality, and in addition thereto, if the wages that are generally accepted as current are not fair and reasonable wages, our officers will fix as the wage a wage that is fair and reasonable rather than the current wage. I must say that in my experience in the Labour department in the last four cur five years I have run across no difficulties, or difficulties so indifferent that I have not charged my memory with them, where the wages fixed by the department have not been fair and reasonable. Sometimes they are the current wages. They are never lower than the current wages, and very frequently they have been higher.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: Would the minister indicate the nature of the amendment he proposed? I have only just come in.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: The amendment has been withdrawn.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: What was its nature?

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: It was proposed to strike from the third line of section 2 the words "from time to time" and insert in lieu thereof the words "at the date of the contract when such work is being performed by contract." It was pointed out by the leader of the opposition that a contract for a considerable period of time might well work a hardship upon employees, and upon his suggestion the amendment was withdrawn.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Just a word on this olause as to wages that are fair and reasonable. Evidently the contractors would have to have some indication of the wages they would have to pay before they could tender on the contract. They may have tendered intending
to pay the prevailing wage. That is the wage which the fair wage officer must take into consideration. I understand that it means that the fair wage officer must find out the prevailing rate, how many employers there are in the district and how -many pay such and such a rate, and if more pay a certain rate than another rate the rate paid by the greatest number is accepted as the prevailing rate. When and how is the government going to come to the conclusion that the rate being paid is not a fair and reasonable rate. Who is going to determine it? Is it going to be determined after a complaint from some of the employees on a particular work, or is the fair wage officer going to investigate and report to the government as to the wages being paid?

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: The fair wage officers of the Department of Labour determine what the fair wages shall be with respect to any contract, and in determining what fair wages shall be they certainly inquire into what are the current wages for competent workmen in the class of work to be performed. They undoubtedly inquire as to whether or not there is a prevailing rate of wages and in all cases they are charged with responsibility of seeing that the wages paid are fair and reasonable. If the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis) will investigate, as he undoubtedly has, the wages paid od federal contracts, he will find that very frequently the fair wage officers of the department have insisted upon the payment of wages which were higher than the current or prevailing rate-"prevailing" is not used in the statute-in order that the wages paid may be fair and reasonable. That has been the policy of the department and I trust it will be the policy in the future.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: That section has been in use for many years.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: In the case of a dispute would the Department of Labour accept the fair wage act of the particular province in which the dispute .might occur?

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
It is not likely that the
dominion would cast aside the judgment of a province with respect to a matter of that kind but the dominion would not be prepared to accept the statement of a province as to what was fair and reasonable wages. All these matters would be inquired into from all angles, including what was the judgment of the province as to what was fair and reasonable wages.

Fair Wages and Hours oj Labour

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
There might be two sets of
wages for the same class of work and difficulty might arise. In order that the uniformity of pay within a province should be maintained I think the government should be prepared to accept the judgment of the provincial authorities as to what was considered fair and proper within the province.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
In my judgment that is
just what the dominion government should not do. I do not think the dominion government should be committed to paying wages which are high or which are low simply because a province has adopted a scale and considers it as the proper current rate. The endeavour of the federal government is to see that fair and reasonable wages are paid on federal works. If the hon. member thinks over this matter I believe he will banish from his mind the idea that the true intent and meaning of this legislation would be brought about by the federal government subscribing to the judgment of the nine provinces of Canada as to what was fair and reasonable wages.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Government contracts for work subject to certain conditions.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Is it not a
general rule that where the eight hour day prevails the forty-four hour week also prevails?

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: I have no doubt that the forty-four hour week does prevail in some undertakings but there are many industrial undertakings where it does not prevail.

I should like to repeat

In the harbour of Montreal there are several thousand men who work only during the summer, some of them for only a part of the summer. Instead of having a time limit placed upon their work they are anxious to work longer hours as that provides compensation for the time they do not work. While in theory the eight hour day and the forty-four hour week may be very nice, when it comes to practice in these times we are much more concerned about the people who are not working rather than limiting the hours of those who are working. I notice that subsection (b) of this section provides for cases such as I have mentioned, when it states:
-or except in cases of emergency as may be approved by the minister.
The minister was very kind in meeting the suggestions I made when we were dealing with the other bill, and I should like to know from him whether this bill is to have the same effect. Will the government or the minister be able to allow men working in harbours, for instance, to work more than eight hours a day or forty-four hours a week? I have been greatly interested in the theoretical social reform legislation with which we have been busy for most of the session but when I go back to my people I find that they are not looking for minimum wages, they are looking for wages of any kind; they are not complaining because they have to work too much, it is the other way around, they are afraid that their week will be shortened. maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext: The subject raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South has been debated many times in connection with both this and former legislation. It is my view that the government cannot fix wages where materials, supplies and equipment are being purchased, that is, traced back to the various factories or departments of factories where these things are being manufactured. This would not be practicable in the first place. If the federal government are paying higher wages, as they very frequently and indeed in most cases do, than industry is paying or able to pay; in other words, if they ai'e giving at least some lead to those who are able to pay higher wages, then, if they were to undertake the project their activities back behind the actual construction, because we are dealing with construction of buildings, into the wages that are being paid in the manufacture of supplies that go into such buildings and that are not made on the ground, I think we would be in great difficulty and I doubt seriously whether this could be administered.

maintopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Perhaps in some cases it might not be possible to trace materials back far enough, but in many cases, especially in connection with building, this could be most readily done. For instance stone comes from a certain quarry. There are certain quarries in which fair wages are paid; there are others in which unfair wages are paid. Surely it is quite possible for the Dominion government to purchase only from those quarries where fair wages are being paid. The same thing is true with regard to steel used in certain building construction. We have some factories in which it is known fair wages are paid; there are others in which it is generally known unfair wages are paid and sweating conditions prevail. I think the report of the price spreads commission
recommends that action be taken by the government along this line and even goes so far as to suggest general legislation so that there would be something in the nature of a white list and a label provided in order that we might know whether articles are being produced under fair conditions. The opinion of the law officers of the crown and of very profound men who are students of constitutional law is that if a forty-four hour week is placed in the statute itself, that leaves it open to impeachment; but in order to make it possible that a forty-four hour week or less may prevail in connection with the expenditure of moneys by a province-and I cite the province as an instance-where the dominion contributes to that expenditure, provision is made that an agreement be en-

Fair Wages and Hours of Labour
tered into pursuant to the terms of this legislation, and in that agreement the condition may be imposed as to working hours per week. In other words the measure is inviolate; it provides that the working hours per week shall not exceed forty-eight, which we believe to be constitutional, and the stipulation can carry through into the agreement when one is entered into: Here is the dominion's contribution to you, but we will give it only on condition that you subscribe to, say, a forty-four hour week. They can either take it or leave it. In my view this places the legislation beyond reach of impeachment and places within the hands of the dominion government or the executive, as the case may be, the right to impose those conditions in the agreement.

I do not think it is a constitutional question at all. The minister has not shown how it affects the constitution. He simply asserts that he has had certain advice.
