Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour) moved the second reading of Bill No. 79, to amend the Combines Investigation Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Morand in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.
Perhaps the minister will explain the bill. Is it exactly in conformity with the recommendations of the price spreads commission?

Yes, in substance. It is to amend the present act to give effect to certain of the recommendations made by the price spreads commission, but the major change is to transfer the powers at present

invested in the registrar and the Minister of Labour to a federal industry commission, which it is contemplated establishing under the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act. Then the remainder of the amendments are merely to bring the present act into conformity by substituting the commission for the registrar, and I believe in one or tivo instances for the minister, so that throughout the present act the amendments will conform.
I believe under the present act the minister takes the ground that the report of the registrar need not be made public. Under the amended law will all reports of the commission be made public?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member will recall that in connection with the tariff board we had a long discussion about this matter. The two acts will be read together, so far as that is concerned, and the tariff board would be the judge as to whether it was not in the public interest or unfair to the individual to have the investigation published. That is, obviously everything is not published, but everything is not secret, and the board shall be the determining tribunal with respect to that feature of the matter. That is what has been determined in the past in connection with the Tariff Board Act.

It seems to me that this is distinctly a retrograde step, because under the Combines Investigation Act which we have had in the past at least the commissioner's findings were made public. Some of us have claimed that the registrar's findings should also be made public. Apparently, however, we are now to have a new commission, namely the tariff board, which shall have power to state whether or not its findings shall be made public.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No; I think the hon. member misunderstood me. I referred to the evidence, not the findings.
I am speaking about the findings of the commission and my question was as to whether or not the findings were to be made public. Did I understand the Prime Minister correctly?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No. I was dealing with the evidence. The hon. member will recall that a great deal of discussion took place on this point when the tariff board was set up. The findings of that board are made public.

My question is whether or not the findings of the commission will be made public.

Combines Investigation Act

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Not the evidence. At the present time the minister takes the ground that the reports of the registrar need not be made public. The question was whether or not under the new arrangement the reports of the commission would be made public.
Yes, they will be made public.

After reading the act I would not think that to be so. In the Combines Investigation Act the matter is covered in two or three sections. Reports of commissioners were made public, unless there was a provision in the report recommending against publicity, but the section dealing with reports of the registrar was silent. The minister took the view that the section being silent he had no authority to make the reports public. I know however it was the view of members of the price spreads commission that that opinion was incorrect, that the act being silent the minister had a discretion in the matter and could make the reports of- the registrar public or otherwise, as he wished. In Bill No. 86, providing for the establishment of a dominion trade and industry commission, section 28 states:
The commission shall within fifteen days after making any report, recommendation or finding under this act make the same public in such manner as seems desirable unless the commission is unanimously of the opinion that the public interest would not be served by publication or that the public interest would be better served by withholding publication.
(2) Wherever possible the commission shall with the report, recommendation or finding make public the reason and the facts upon which the decision is based.
I do not know at this time whether that section applies to reports made under the Combines Investigation Act, but I assume that is the section that applies.
It will apply.

Yes, it will apply when the two bills are passed. We gave some thought to the matter of publicity when we were considering the evidence placed before the price spreads commission. The members of that body were of the opinion that there was no good reason why reports should not always be .made public.
Of the registrar?

Yes. There might be
reasons why all of the evidence in a case should not be made public, but we concluded that there was no good reason why every report should not be made public. There are a great many instances where six persons
apply to the registrar, under the Combines Investigation Act, alleging that a combine exists and asking for an investigation. The registrar looks into the facts and circumstances and decides that the six persons who signed the application did not fully go into the matter, that they are proceeding on hearsay evidence and that they are wrong. In such event he would make a short report indicating that there was no reason why there should be any investigation. From time to time such reports are made. It is a very common thing for a few individuals from one part of Canada or another to write the registrar and allege the existence of a combine. Upon looking into the facts the registrar sometimes decides that what these people allege to be a combine does not contain the statutory elements of a combine, and makes a report to that effect. That would be the end of the matter. There is no reason why those reports should not be made public; they cannot possibly hurt anybody. When the registrar finds that the facts are such as to warrant an inquiry he may proceed to investigate and may in the end find that a combine exists. It may be that on some occasions a court may find that a combine did not exist. Only once in the history of the administration of the Combines Investigation Act has a judge found that a combine did not exist when in the first instance the registrar had found that it did; in every .other case the court has corroborated the finding of the registrar. It seems to me rather theoretical and fanciful to state that in publishing the findings any injustice would be done. An intolerable condition exists when we permit the making of expensive and important inquiries into alleged combines and have the reports kept secret. That is what has happened.
We took enough evidence before the price spreads commission to know that in the rubber trade there is a condition of affairs which apparently constitutes a combine. We tried to get the report which was made in connection with this industry, but could not get it; it was kept secret, and has not been published. I can, see no reason why it should not be published. It is most important, if matters of this kind are to be considered intelligently by governments or parliaments that publicity be given to them. I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is asking for full publicity of reports, and' if I understand his position correctly I strongly support it. I am sorry the necessary provision to bring that about is not made in this bill.
Combines Investigation Act

Mr. WOOD8WORTH: Decidedly I believe in such publicity, but I was attempting to get at the facts of the case. A few moments ago I asked the minister if all the reports would be made public, and apparently he was not quite sure. In the meantime the Prime Minister stated that in the case of the tariff board the evidence was not made public. I had not been talking about the evidence but about the report, and I again asked the minister, who stated that all reports would be made public. Then the Iron, member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) read section 28 of the trade and industry commission bill, and I understood the minister to say that it was that act that applied in this case. If it does then it is quite obvious that the publication of these reports is not automatic but within the discretion of the commission, and in enacting this legislation we are taking a retrograde step because in the past, although we could not get the registrar's reports, at least we got the reports of the commission. Now apparently the commission itself may decide whether or not it gives us any report. I am strongly of the opinion that we should have full publicity with regard to these matters.

I just want to add to what I said that the evidence before the price spreads commission revealed a startling concentration of business in Canada, great numbers of large corporations and what the experts call monopolies and quasi-monopolies. Times are changing. It may have been quite proper twenty or thirty years ago to be very careful as to what publicity you gave to matters of this kind, but it is highly important in these latter days that the public have all the facilities possible for coping with these great concentrations of industry, and to that end it seems to me important that the public be acquainted with the true state of affairs. The act is being amended not only to cover combines but to give better facilities for coping with monopolies such as mergers and the like, and it is exceedingly important that the public be acquainted at once on the conclusion of an investigation with the true state of affairs. If, for instance, eighty-five per cent of the packing industry gets into the hands of one company, which is what would happen if two of the largest companies were to merge at the present time, that is a fact which the public should know, and know at once. It would be revealed by an investigation under the Combines Act as amended, and it is not a fact that the commission should have the discretion to keep to themselves. There is no danger that I can see about publicity. The danger that always 
used to be urged was that publicity might prejudice the mind of the public in the event of a criminal prosecution, but an official report is no more likely to do that than the irresponsible reports in the newspapers-not nearly as likely, because what the registrar or what the commission finds about these great combinations and monopolies and quasimonopolies is quite certain to be true. I would urge that the government provide for full publicity of these reports rather than leave it to the discretion of the investigating commission.

The question of what sort of report, whether the report of the registrar's inquiry or of a commissioner, should be made public and be given publicity has been the subject of discussion since the first legislation was enacted in 1910, and upon its subsequent reenactment with amendments thirteen years afterwards. Rightly or wrongly, the Combines Investigation Act at present in force is silent with respect to publicity to be given to the report of the registrar, whether that report be a final or an interim one. It is equally true that since the act was amended in 1023 the practice of the Department of Labour and of the federal government has been to treat the silence of the legislation with respect to publicity as constituting the foundation of proper practice, that these investigations and inquiries should not be made public.

I have in my possession a
report dealing with the P.A.T.A,, a report that was made by the registrar. Two reports were made1 in 1925 and 1926, one by the registrar and one by the commissioner, and the, registrar's report was printed and published.

It may be that the registrar's report was published) but I am stating that the general practice was not to make them public. The act, of course, did and does make provision for publication of a commissioner's report. When the Combines Act was before parliament in 1923 a long discussion took place with respect to its operation and) with respect to what was expected of it in the way of curbing combines and monopolies which were against the public interest and in restraint of trade. Great things were expected of the combines act, and so far as the act went I think it did bring about some sort of useful progress. But there is no manner of doubt that white the present combines act was upon the statute book great combines came into existence. I am not prepared to condemn them as detrimental to the public interest, or to commend them as the kind of monopoly that is in the

Combines Investigation Act
public interest-for there are the two kinds, as everyone admits. But with respect to the publication of a preliminary inquiry into the business of people where full facilities are given for such inquiry and where it is expected that a full and confidential disclosure shall be made of all the intimacies of the business, I have no doubt that that was the consideration that influenced, those in the past to be extremely careful about publishing to the world and to the man's competitors the complexities and the inner workings of his business. I am sure that every member of this House of Commons could have his own private business investigated and would welcome complete publicity with respect to his every activity, and that every member would emerge as pure as the driven snow, but at the same time there were those in years gone by who thought that to make public a confidential and complete disclosure of all a man's business was something that should not be done in a hurry, that the information should not be just poured out through a funnel for his competitors. I believe that was the argument that then prevailed, but as the hon. member for Hants-Kings has said, since the investigation of last year, times have changed. We are undoubtedly in changing times, and perhaps it is proper and right that these things should be published to the world, whether they are right or whether they are wrong, on the principle I assume that if a man is right his business should be known to everybody, and if he is wrong he should be pilloried at once. These are just observations that you can take in any way you like. On section 6-Discrimination in trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Returning to this bill which was partly discussed on a former occasion, I think I should put on record the recommendation of the price spreads commission with regard to the matters with which it deals. At page 135 of the report of the royal commission, certain amendments to the criminal code are recommended. I need not read that section. On page 246 there is another recommendation in regard to fraudulent advertising, dealt with by clause 4 of the bill, but the portion of the report which I desire particularly to read is at page 270. I will start in the middle of the page:
We suggest that practices should be prohibited as unfair which are characterized by bad' faith, fraud, misrepresentation, or oppression; which are resorted to for the purpose of destroying competition or eliminating a competitor; which facilitate the development of monopoly; or which destroy fair corn-competitive opportunity and prevent the survival of those who can organize and carry on the production of goods most efficiently. It is in this sense that the word "unfair" should be used in the act.
Without attempting to restrict the application of this test of "unfairness" by the commission, we feel that certain practices which we have examined should very definitely be considered "unfair" under the act. They are so widespread and generally condemned that their complete prohibition by the commission is justified. We refer specifically to-
1.	discriminatory discounts, rebates and allowances,
2.	territorial price discrimination and predatory price cutting.
The reference in the extract which I have just read is to the trade commission which is recommended in this report and is not to the criminal code. Clauses were drafted to carry into effect that recommendation for the purpose of inserting them in the federal trade commission measure, but immediately we had

done so we realized that our troubles were beginning. In view of the decision of the judicial committee of the privy council) in respect to the Board of Commerce Act and the Combines and Fair Prices Act, if we bad placed in that bill prohibitory sections in regard to the matters recommended in the report, according to the opinion of the law officers of the department they would have fallen to the ground1 as ultra vires; they could not be supported1. It is true that the general regulation of trade and commerce is, under the British North America Act, within the competence of this parliament; but the moment you go to the point of interfering with private rights, the moment you begin to fix prices, to interfere with contracts or matters of that kind, you have gone, according to the decision of the judicial committee of the privy council, beyond the realm of the regulation of trade and commerce. Property and civil rights within a province are within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial legislature, and for that reason these sections which were drafted originally for the trade and commerce bill were omitted from it. While there was serious doubt as to our right to pass such legislation-and indeed it was not doubtful; it was definitely decided that we had no such right-we have the right in this parliament to pass criminal laws as we see fit to do, and these particular sections were therefore transferred into the bill to amend the criminal code of Canada.
The question of course arises whether the amendments which we now submit are really in their pith and substance, which is the language used in so many of the judicial committee's judgments, of criminal legislation. We submit they are in so far as they are for the protection of the public, for the good of the community and to frustrate unfair practices by traders throughout Canada.
Let me, after making that preliminary statement, place upon the record the opinion which I had not with me when this matter was before the house on a former occasion. At that time I read the opinion of Mr. Tilley, K.C., upon these sections, and it will be remembered that he pronounced upon them as follows: that section 4 of the bill was good and within the competence of parliament. In regard to section 5 he said: " I think it is intra vires; in regard to section 6, paragraph (a) is of doiibtful validity, paragraph
(b)	is valid, and paragraph (c) is valid." Such is the opinion, in brief, of Mr. Tilley, K.C.
I desire to place upon the record the opinion of Mr. Geoffrion, K.C., in regard to

Criminal Code Amendment
the same section. His opinion under date of May 15, 1935, to the Deputy Minister of Justice is as follows:
Sir,-In conformity with your letter of the 6th instant, I have read the bill to amend the criminal code, sections 4, 5 and 6, with a view of giving my opinion as to the powers of parliament to adopt it.	_	_
I believe this is good criminal legislation, therefore within the dominion's powers, except possibly paragraph (a) and (lb) of section 415A as enacted by section 5 of the bill.
I take it that, generally, these paragraphs aim at punishment for violation of provincial legislation respecting minimum wages and maximum hours. Of course, there can be no doubt in so far as federal legislation on that subject is concerned. The majority of eases would, however, be covered by provincial laws because the subject of minimum wages and maximum hours of labour is, it seems to me, normally a provincial subject.
I know the dominion parliament has already claimed power to decree punishment for the violation of a provincial statute; section 164 of the criminal code is an example of that and this has never been challenged but I doubt the validity of such an enactment in view of section 92 of the British North America Act. paragraph 15, which gives to the provincial legislature exclusive legislative power concerning the imposition of punishments for enforcing any law of the province, et cetera, et cetera. If the dominion can decree a punishment for the breach of a, provincial law. it can do so whether the province has decreed one or not. The legislative power in that respect ceases to toe exclusive, notwithstanding the terms of the British North America Act and the dominion statute must prevail so that the provincial legislature enacting mandatory or prohibitory provisions will be exposed to have a punishment attached to its orders quite different from the one it desired. The power to order and the power to punish for disobedience should logically be united.
I would think the words "criminal law" in section 91 should be restricted by paragraph 15 of section 92. just as "marriage" in section 91 is restricted by "solemnization of marriage" in section 92. The general words in the assignment to the dominion in both cases being restricted by the special exclusive assignment to the province.
I do not think however, that these provisions, if unconstitutional, would affect the validity of the rest of the act.
Yours truly,
A. Geoffrion.
Now it will be noted that Mr. Geoffrion states as his opinion that sections 4 and 6 of the bill are within the jurisdiction of this parliament, and section 5 is also valid except possibly subsections (a) and (b). As to the contention of Mr. Geoffrion that we would be imposing penalties in regard to laws of the provinces in respect of which penalties are already imposed, it is to be noted that for many years. I think since 1888, our criminal code has contained clause 164, which I am going to read:
Everyone is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to one year's imprisonment, who, 92582-2211
without legal excuse, disobeys any act of the parliament of Canada or of any legislature in Canada by wilfully doing any act which it forbids, or omitting to do any act which it requires to be done, unless some penalty or other mode of punishment is expressly provided by law.
That section has never been directly challenged in the courts. If anyone thinks it is a doubtful section, as Mr. Geoffrion does, at any rate it has stood the test of forty-five years and I think more than that. I know that an opinion was given on that question by the late Hon. Edward Blake, an eminent lawyer, who while Minister of Justice affirmed our right to impose these penalties notwithstanding penalties imposed by provincial laws, and that opinion has been followed in the department ever since.
Let me summarize the position. I leave out section 4 for the moment, because according 'to all legal opinions that we have obtained, both of the law officers of the department and of the two eminent counsel I have mentioned, section 4 is within the competence of the parliament of Canada. With regard to section 5, Mr. Geoffrion entertains doubts as to subclauses (a) and (b). Mr. Tilley expresses 'the opinion that the whole section is within the legislative competence of this parliament. In regard to section 6 Mr. Tilley expresses doubts as to subclause (a) but says subclauses Ob) and
(c)	are valid. Mr. Geoffrion expresses the opinion that the whole of section 6 is within the compeitence of this parliament. On a former occasion it was very much criticized that the government should introduce into this house a 'bill in regard to which there should be some doubt expressed. It is not the first time such a course has been taken. There is doubt u,p to the present time about many of our constitutional rights, which have never been tested, and some provincial rights too. If on account of these doubts the provinces withhold their hands and pass no legislation, and if we are to do the same here, the result of course is stalemate and no legislation 'occupies the field. My hon. friend the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is not in his place, but he will well remember section 1025 of the criminal code, which abolished all appeals in criminal cases to the judicial committee of the privy council. That was a section of doubtful validity which was passed toy this parliament. In 1928 when it came before the judicial committee they held it as ultra vires of this parliament-as bad, void. When the statute of Westminster was passed by the British parliament and reenacted in this parliament, section 1025 was again passed by this house and the senate and
Criminal Code Amendment

became law, but recently it has been challenged again before the judicial committee, and on Thursday or Triday I think of last week a judgment was given maintaining the right of the parliament of Canada to enact section 1025.
Did they know it was doubtful when they enacted it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It was always looked upon as doubtful.
Was it so expressed here in parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is an opinion in the Department of Justice that it was doubtful. I could enumerate a score of acts in regard to which there was douibt. I am going to mention one because it was up in the house to-day, that is the Canada Grain Act. When that law was enacted the late Mr. Justice Newcombe expressed the opinion that many of the sections were of doubtful validity. Subsequently the act was before the Supreme Court of Canada and certain sections were held invalid, as beyond the legislative jurisdiction of this parliament. But in that case the supreme court- suggested a remedy to us. They said: If you declare the elevators to be works for the general advantage of Canada, you might overcome the difficulty. In the following session, to cure the difficulty and remove the doubts, parliament passed an act to declare these elevators to be works for the general advantage of Canada. But there are some sections of the act not yet without doubt, and in order to remove further doubt or make the act secure so far as it might be possible to do so, this ingenious clause was put in at the end:
234. If it is found that parliament has exceeded its powers in the enactment of one or more of the provisions of this act, none of the other or remaining provisions of the act shall therefore be held to be inoperative or ultra vires, but the latter provisions shall stand -as if they had been originally enacted as separate and independent enactments and as the only provisions of the act; the inter)-' tion of parliament being to give independent effect to the extent of its powers to every enactment and provision in this act contained.
I submit the present measure in the form in which it is drawn is a serious attempt to carry out as far as it possibly -can be done by this parliament the recommendations of the price spreads commission in regard to unfair trade practices. The best legal opinion we can get on the subject says that if we place these sections in the trade commission act, as recommended in the report, they will be ultra vires of the powers of this 
parliament as an interference with property and civil rights within the various provinces. If we place them in the criminal code, however, and treat this as criminal legislation, probably they will stand fire, although as I have elaborated doubt has been expressed in the opinions of Mr. Tilley and Mr. Geoffrion. The -other sections of the code, of course, are not open to that constitutional conflict, but sections 4, 5 and 6 of this act are prepared with an eye to carrying out the recommendations of -the price spreads commission.
I would ask this committee to give serious consideration to these -clauses. I know they were rather roundly denounced the other night, but that does not get rid of them. They are entitled to serious consideration and in the main according to the best legal opinions obtainable, they are valid. Some of the subsections are called not invalid but doubtful. That is the spirit in which this bill is submitted to the house at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, I think there could be written across the face of this bill, particularly sections 5 and 6, "sic transit gloria reform." If this is the best this government can do to implement all the promises contained in the radio speeches which were made last- January, then it does seem to me that His Excellency the Governor General would be well advised to come down and dissolve this house.
I am going to deal with what my hon. friend the Minister of Justice has said in regard to the legal aspect of the matter, but I hope that the discussion will not entirely centre around the legal phases of this bill. This is just -another instalment of the series of anti-climaxes to those radio speeches of January last, which has been furnished to this house during the last three -or four months. From time to time we have had shreds and patches of the resounding sentiments whitfh were -expressed on that occasion. We have had the unemployment insurance act, which was broadcast so as to hold out the hope to the working people and the unemployed of -this country that it was going to solve all their problems. But when the unemployment insurance act was brought down we found that it did not benefit anybody for a year at least; that it would not assist in the slightest in connection with the unemployment which exists in this country, but -that it would only help those who were already employed and who were able to pay the assessments for the time set out in that act. We also found that it left out three of

Criminal Code Amendment
the four primary industries of .the Dominion of Canada.
Then we had the eight hour day bill before us this afternoon, the law with regard to hours of labour on, public works. In either the last or the next to last section of the bill we find that the act will not come into force until May 1, 1936. Then there was the Companies Act. We were going to do away with no par shares, those things which are Said to have been the delusion of the investor. The amendment to the Companies Act has been brought down; no par shares are not struck out. They will continue to be issued notwithstanding the strictures of the Prime Minister regarding them. The dole was a rotten thing according to the radio speeches, but the dole still exists in Canada and we have been voting goodly amounts of relief money for that purpose. Now finally the report of the price spreads commission is crystallized into a few sections which appear in this act, and notwithstanding the statement which was made during the radio broadcasts with regard to the open market place, I would almost think that the open market place is going to continue. During the course of those speeches last January the Prime Minister said:
You would' agree that free competition and the open market place, as they were known in the old days, have lost their place in the system, and that the only substitute for them, in these modern times, is government regulation and control.
And, according to this act, that government regulation and control is going to consist of making it a crime for a man to give a greater discount to one man than to another.
I want to deal for a .moment with section- 6, which has been, referred to by the Minister of Justice, and the legality of which has been discussed, in order to give the committee the effect of what section 6 really provides. Section 6 says in substance that if Mr. A is doing business and gives to Mr. B a greater discount on a similar quantity of goods than the discount which he gives to Mr. C, Mr. A is guilty of a crime and should go to gaol. It does not make any difference that Mr. A is giving that larger discount to Mr. B in order to meet a price which Mr. B had been quoted by somebody else; Mr. A is still a criminal because of the fact that he met the price of his competitor. There is nothing in the act which intimates that Mr. A cannot give Mr. B a lower price than he gives Mr. C; all that is provided is that he must not give a greater discount. That is to say, while he cannot quote a price of $100 and give one man ten per
cent off and another man fifteen per cent off, there is nothing in the section which says he cannot quote one man a price of $80 and another man a price of $85, because that is not giving a discount. Neither is there anything in the section to suggest that he could not take a base price of $80 and say to one man, "I will give you these goods at $80 plus ten per cent," and to another man, "I will give you these goods at $80 plus fifteen per cent"; in that case he has not committed any crime because he has not given any rebate or discount.
I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, that we ought seriously to consider the legislation we put on the statute books. All we are doing here is to make law evaders of the people of the Dominion of Canada when we pass sections of that kind, and I am leaving out altogether the question of the validity of the act. I say on the construction of the act itself it is nothing less than a snare and a delusion so far as the mercantile people of this country are concerned, and nothing less than a sham and mockery so far as the relief of the consumer is concerned. There is nothing real in it. People can readily evade the law; anyone can read it and see that he can easily get around a section like this, but still the section is put in in deference to some of those who feel that if they could have their feelings salved by having at least a little of the report of the price spreads commission carried out that would at least save their faces. I submit that a section which prevents an honest trader from meeting competition and makes no allowance for savings in sales costs on account of selling a large volume is not the sort of section which should be written into the criminal law of the Dominion of Canada. We had1 a commission which cost this country $500,000. If this is the best this government can bring down in implementing the report of that commission then that $500,000 has been worse than wasted. I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, that a section of this kind is just silly; it is just meddling, that is all; interfering and irritating without doing the slightest good.
I am not the only one who holds that opinion. The other night I noticed, and I intended to read, an editorial which appeared not in a Liberal organ but in a newspaper which is supposed to support this government, the Montreal Star. It was referring to the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) when he introduced this bill, when he admitted that some of these sections were of doubtful validity. This is what the Star said:
Doubtless our parliamentarians, both inside and outside the cabinet, will have this
Criminal Code Amendment

phase of the matter well in view. The senate just the other day had to hold up and rewrite a government measure which had passed the commons. Last week we heard a minister introduce a bill with the amazing statement that he was not quite sure of its constitutionality.
That was the Minister of Justice, in connection with the bill we are now considering.
Surely now there will be an end to this sort of thing. Parliament will have the full support of the people in adopting legislation which promises to ameliorate, even to a small degree, the genuinely distressing conditions under which our people are to-day living, but it will not earn any public gratitude by driving through sham relief measures which profess to work miracles but which will lead only to chaos, disappointment, a further paralysis of business and the general confusion which to-day pervades the United States.
I do not think any more apt words could have been used concerning the bill before us to-night, in view of what the Minister of Justice has just said, than the words I have just read. We remember what occurred in the United States. Chaos and confusion reign because a law was enacted; business had to set up new machinery and make expensive readjustments to meet it and when attempts were made to enforce it it was held to be without legal foundation. The result is that the man who played the game and lived up to the letter of this invalid law has been penalized because his competitor had nerve enough to disregard it. The same situation will arise in Canada, one which would lead only to disappointment. The people who do attempt to live up to it will be prejudiced and, will be at a disadvantage with their competitors.
Now, with regard to the legal situation I am not going to attempt to discuss the opinions which the Minister of Justice has read to-night. I should be perfectly satisfied, had we definite opinions from either of the gentlemen whom he has quoted. I should be satisfied if we had a definite opinion from the Department of Justice itself. But the minister a few nights ago, upon introducing ;he bill, and in a discussion in committee ntimated clearly that he himself held the gravest doubts as to its validity. We do not aave to go farther than that. At page 3166 of Hansard he makes the statement that the opinion of the law officers of the crown is that section 5 presents some difficulties. He has now brought forward Mr. Geoffrion's opinion in which it is stated that that gentleman is doubtful about the validity of clauses
(a)	and (b) of section 5. And the minister tells us the Department of Justice was doubtful about all the clauses of section 5. On

the other hand Mr. Tilley felt they could be supported; so there we are. There is no doubt that the Minister of Justice and his department are doubtful about section 5. In fact the minister is doubtful about the whole section and Mr. Geoffrion is doubtful about subsections (a) and (b), and still it is proposed to pass this bill.
The Minister of Justice has said that if we do not legislate and if the province does not legislate, both being fearful of our jurisdiction, what will happen? I say to him, and I think he will agree with me that there is no reason in the world why the province could not legislate in connection with subsection (a) and
(b)	of section S. No person has suggested that the province has not the right to legislate with regard to employment of persons at rates of wages less than the minimum rates fixed by law or public authority. There is no difficulty about the province legislating in that matter. ' Up to this time we have assumed that the provinces have had jurisdiction with respect to minimum wages. In fact, all the parliamentary utterances from the Prime Minister down for a long time past have indicated that the provinces were the bodies which had the jurisdiction with regard to wage rates. Therefore there should be no question that the province has power to legislate with regard to the matters contained in subsection (a) of the new section 4I15A and the same applies to subsection (b). The minister's fears about nobody being able to legislate if we do not attempt to do it here seem quite groundless.
If I were permitted to express an opinion about subsection (c) of section 5 I should have thought it was valid. That is to say, in connection with the subsection which reads:
(c)	falsifies any employment record required to be kept by law or any competent public authority;
I should have thought that falsification was a criminal offence, and that in its very nature it was morally wrong and detrimental to the public interest. But subsections (a) and (b) are different. They have to do with matters [DOT]of contract and civil rights. Then, subsection
(d)	reads:
(d)	punches a time clock with intent to
deceive;
That would seem to be a crime. Then, as to subsections (e), (f), (g), and (h) I would say that subsection (e) may contain an element of crime but, as the law officers of the crown have properly indicated, subsections (f), (g), and (h) seem to deal with matters essentially having to do with private contracts.

Criminal Code Amendment
I now turn to section 6 of the bill. What are the 'opinions respecting this section to which the Minister of Justice has referred. He stated in no uncertain terms that he had doubts as to the validity of this section-and when I refer to section 6 I direct your attention particularly to subsection (a), with which I have just dealt, and which makes it a crime for a man. to give a greater discount to one man than to his competitor. The Minister of Justice has doubts about this section. The following opinion expressed by Mr. Tilley appears at page 3166 of Hansard:
Subsection (1) of section 6 is, I think, of very doubtful validity, but sections (2) and (3) are, I think, valid.
By subsection (1) he means, I .think, subsection (a). At a later point, at page 3167 of Hansard, the opinion of Mr. Tilley is cited as follows:
All I can say is that in my opinion the subsections is of very doubtful validity, and I incline to the view it is invalid.
Here he is again speaking of subsection (a) of section 6. I do not think we need much more than that. However, let us turn to the statement of the Minister of Justice as it appears at page 3168 of Hansard. This is what the minister says:
I am giving the committee an opportunity of passing an opinion on the point. I think myself that they would be very inefficacious even if they were passed. I do not believe you could ever support a prosecution on them because you never could prove your case.
What is the use of our passing legislation of that kind? Why waste our time on it? First we have the opinion of Mr. Tilley that the subsections are doubtful, then we have the opinion of the Minister of Justice that he has grave doubts; then we have the opinions of the law officers of the crown that there is doubt. On top of that we have the opinion of the Minister of Justice that in any event it would be inefficacious.
I submit it is time we go to something more substantial than writing formal crimes into law books, knowing in the first instance that there are grave doubts as to the validity of the statutes enacted and graver doubts as to the possibility of securing convictions under them. I should have thought the Minister of Justice would have withdrawn these sections as to which doubts have been expressed by these eminent jurists. I submit for the consideration of this committee and that of the Minister of Justice that we had better devote our attention to something which holds in it more hope for the urgent problems of the people of this dominion than does the legislation before us.
I .conclude my observations by quoting a statement which appeared in a letter written last fall by the Prime Minister to one of his colleagues, upon which occasion he pointed out the danger of raising the hopes of people with regard to legislation of doubtful constitutional validity. Writing to the former Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), the Prime Minister said:
In due course a committee of eleven was appointed and you were elected chairman. From that time the committee had an absolutely free hand and no effort of any kind, shape or form was made to in any way limit or restrict its activities except that on more than one occasion we pointed out to you the danger of creating in the minds of those interested, especially in the retail business, the impression that parliament could provide a remedy for the conditions of which they complained in view of the decisions of the courts as to the jurisdiction of provincial legislatures over contracts and price fixing.
I commend that passage to you, Mr. Chairman, and the committee. I believe we may well take note of it and the warning contained therein, namely, not to take our time in the passage of legislation of doubtful validity, and the attempt by a stroke of a pen to make the people of Canada conform to some idealistic standard of business ethics' couched in such general language as to prohibit perfectly legitimate and straightforward business transactions, and which cannot be enforced.
I submit to the Minister of Justice that the sections which he is advised by these eminent jurists are invalid or of doubtful validity ought to be withdrawn, so that we may get on with something more practical and useful.

Mr. Chairman, may I make bold to attempt to reply to some of the objections raised by the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), the critic of the opposition. I wonder whether he has made it clear even to himself what his plan is so far as the carrying out of the report of the price spreads commission is concerned.
Ask some of your own friends.

This aittack is a fair example of the guerilla warfare that is being carried on by the Liberal party throughout Canada, and a very considerable section of the financially interested press, so far as implementing the report of the price spreads commission is concerned!.
Let me first refer to the quesition of the legality of the amendments. I refer specifically to section 6 of the bill now under discussion. With reference to the opinion expressed by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) quoting

Mr. Tilley as ,to the legality of these sections, I refer the committee to an article which appeared in the Toronto Globe of June 4, under the heading How Great Minds Think Alike.
A new and' remarkable example of identity of thought expression, showing how great legal minds can think, speak and give legal opinions alike, and in strangely similar language, has brightened the annals of Canadian law. It is supplied by two legal opinions-one of the late Hon. Edward Blake, K.C., and one of W. N. Tilley, K.C., regarding the same questions of law submitted for their views at periods forty-five years apart.
Then is quoted the opinion of Mr. Tilley in 1935. His opinion has already been put on record1 in Hansard of this session at page 3166. The article then goes on to quote Mr. Tilley as follows:
The result may be an inconvenient exposure to a double liability, but that possibility affords no argument against the right of the dominion to exercise its powers.
Continuing, the writer of the article in the Globe says:
The same legal questions as to a conflict between dominion and provincial legislation arising out of convictions and penalties for offences under dominion and' provincial laws, within the power of both to legislate upon, arose in two old cases in Ontario in the years 1890 and 1892 respectively.
Mr. Blake-1890.
In one of these-that of Regina versus Stone, in the year 1802, reported in volume 23 of the Ontario Law Reports-the late Mr. Justice Rose, at page 49 of that case, said:
"In my opinion, Mr. Edward Blake, in his argument in Regina versus Wason, correctly stated the law as follows: 'The jurisdiction of the provinces and the dominion overlap. The dominion can declare anything a crime, but this only so as not to interfere with Or exclude the powers of the province of dealing with the same _ thing in its civil aspect and of imposing sanctions for the observance of the law (See No. 15 of section 92) so that, though the result might be an inconvenient exposure to a double liability that possibility is no argument against the right to exercise the power.' In discussing federal jurisdiction as to establishing criminal offences, Lord Atkin states:
The definition is wide and may cover activities which have not hitherto been considered to be criminal. But only those combines are affected which have operated or are likely to operate to the detriment or against the interest of the public whether consumers, producers, or others; and if parliament genuinely determines that commercial activities which can be so described are to be suppressed in the public interest, Their Lordships see no reason why parliament should not make them crimes. "Criminal law" means "the criminal law in its widest sense."
Then is cited the case of the Attorney General of Ontario versus the Hamilton Street Railway, 1903, A.C. 524. Continuing, Lord Atkin says:
It certainly is not confined to what was criminal by the law of England, or of any province in 1867. The power must extend to legislation to make new crimes. Criminal law connotes only the quality of such acts or omissions as are prohibited under appropriate penal provisions by authority of the state. The criminal quality of an act cannot be designed by intuition; nor can it be discovered by reference to any statute but one; Is the act prohibited with penal consequences? .... It appears to Their Lordships to be of little value to seek to confine crimes to a category of acts which by their very _ nature belong to the domain of "criminal jurisprudence"; for the domain of criminal jurisprudence can only be ascertained by examining what acts of any particular period are declared by the state to be crimes, and the only common nature they will be found to possess is that they are prohibited by the state and that those who commit them are punished.

I suppose a person has to have a certain economic philosophy in considering our contemporary life in this country. Most of the commission did not take the socialistic view that competition should be done away with, but rather the view that competition should be preserved, that competition is a most important regulating factor, and that our legislation should be directed to the abjective of preserving fair -competition among our trades and industries. It was brought to the attention of the commission that manufacturers were giving much larger discounts to -corporate department stores and perhaps chain stores-although I would not be certain of my recollection on that point-than they were giving to voluntary chains. The committee will understand what that means. A great department store with immense buying power is able to get a discount of say twelve or fourteen per cent off the list price. A number of independent retailers get together, form a voluntary chain and undertake to buy in just as large quantities, to pay cash and to warehouse, in other words as purchasers to put themselves on exactly the same footing as the corporate purchaser. The commission on price
spreads and mass buying-and I say this with all due respect to the majority of the the commission-spent much time and! effort in exploring conditions* and business practices as they exist. It spent little time in delving into the underlying causes of those conditions and trying to seek out the remedy. It appeared to me that for every evil that was found to exist, the commissioners had in their minds one and1 only one remedy, and that perhaps the most futile of all, namely, to pass a law against the evil. Were some people suffering from what they considered unfair competition on the part of their competitors, unfair trade practices, the commission would suggest the passing of a law against it. Were the farmers not receiving from the packers an adequate price for their cattle or hogs, the idea in the mind of the commission was to pass a law against paying low prices. Did merchants find themselves unable to get the cost of their goods ouib of their customers, the remedy that suggested itself to the commission was to pass a law against price cutting. As I said before, the one remedy that suggested itself to the mind of the commission for every evil was to pass a law against it.
There had arisen in this country a condition where business came almost to a standstill. Merchants found their stocks were not moving; manufacturers were unable to get orders for their goods and had to lay off their men. It seemed to me that this condition was not and could1 not be due to the business practices of any one class of merchants or any one Class of buyers; there must have been an underlying cause for it all; for the business decline was experienced not only by the small buyer but by the large buyer; it was experienced not only by the small manufacturer but by the large manufacturer. Every class in the community experienced the same thing. The cause of the trouble in my opinion was the fact that the primary producers in this country had lost their income. The income of our farmers during the first two years of the

depression was cut in half; fifty per cent of their income had disappeared, while retail prices of the goods they had to buy had fallen only about one or two percent.
That is wrong.

No, it is not wrong. I have the figures before me showing that where the net value of farm production for 1928 was $1,501,000,000, .by 1930 it had fallen to $860,000,000. or almost one-half. The index figure given by the bureau of statistics of retail prices, taking 1926 as the base year, letting 1906 equal 100, stood in 1928 at 98-9 and in 1930 at 99-2; in fact retail prices had actually increased slightly while the price of farm products had dropped almost fifty per cent. That condition did not apply to the farmers only; the same condition prevailed in the fishing industry, the lumber industry and all our basic industries. Was it to be expected that under conditions such as these, business would thrive in this country? How can you expect the Canadian people to buy goods when their incomes are cut in half? The primary producers, farmers, fishermen, lumbermen and so on, constitute perhaps sixty per cent of our population, and with sixty per cent of our population unable to buy goods, everyone in business suffered. It seems to me that the logical remedy for that situation is not to pass laws against price cutting but to find what was the cause of the two price levels which had arisen. Here we have sixty per cent of the people of the country selling their goods at a lower price level, while the things they want to buy are on a higher level, so much so that they cannot buy them. The remedy lies in seeking the cause of that condition and removing it, not in passing laws against price discrimination and unfair trade practices.
To me it seems that one of the principal causes of that situation is the wrong fiscal policy which has been followed by this country. I am not blaming this government alone; it has been the policy of the country for years. But this government accentuated the trouble; it went to the extreme limit when on coming into power it found that prices of primary products were falling, and instead of taking steps to see that the prices of secondary products fell with them, they took steps to prevent that, with the result that retail prices were maintained at practically the former level, or in some cases at a higher level, while the prices of farm products dropped almost forty per cent. Yet a stranger coming to this country and reading
the majority report of the price spreads commission and having no other source of information would have the impression not only that the fiscal policy of the country was in no way to blame for the situation, but that it had actually helped to improve conditions. Nothing could be. further from the truth. The hon. member who just spoke (Mr. Stevens) referred to the price of tomatoes being cut to 70 cents when it should have been 80 to 90 cents. Why was it cut to 70 cents? Did any man cut the price just for the fun of it? It was cut to 70 cents because the people who had those tomatoes had to find a way of getting them into the hands of the consumer. As I said before, a condition arose in which the consumers could not buy the goods, and the merchants were then obliged to find goods at a price which the consumers could pay or not sell them at all. Some influence had to come into the market to force down the price of retail goods to a parity with the price of primary products. When we proceed to legislate against the forcing down of those prices we legislate for conditions which will perpetuate the depression instead of relieving it. Let me give an example. Beans were priced at 5 cents a pound. They were not selling at that price, because people could not pay it; therefore the merchants could not sell the stocks they had, and so could not buy any more from the farmers. The price of beans to the farmer dropped to sixty cents a bushel. Then one of the large chain store concerns said: We think we can clear up this situation. So they advertised beans for sale throughout the country at one cent a pound-that is price slashing for you. What happened? They sold thousands and thousands of bushels of beans at that price. Other merchants had to meet that price; they had to take the loss on the stocks on hand. Such large quantities of beans went into consumption that the market was cleared, the glut was removed and immediately the price began to rise. Now I ask you, was it not better for the farmer, for the consumer, for the merchant, for everyone concerned that the price of beans be slashed as it was so that beans would move into consumption, than that the price be maintained as the merchants were attempting to do, with the result that no one could sell any beans?
Would you apply that argument to wheat?

It not only proposes to send the man to gaol for stealing the time of his employee; it proposes to send him to gaol for working his employee overtime even if he pays him for it. Section 5 says:
Everyone is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years imprisonment or to a fine not exceeding $5,000, or to both imprisonment and' fine who, knowingly-

What does that section contemplate? We do not know what the maximum hours would be; we do not know what would be determined to be a crime in the different provinces, but we know that if any employer permits his employee to work overtime, even if he pays him double time for it, he can be sent to gaol. Let us take a few cases. Suppose a bricklayer is sent by his employer to build a chimney. Suppose when quitting time comes the chimney is almost finished, and he says: "I do not want to come back to-morrow morning and finish this; I will work an extra half hour and finish it to-night." It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that as so far we have had speakers only from the government side and the opposition, possibly it would be well that some of us who belong to neither of these parties should have a word to say on this matter. As I understand it the Liberals take their stand in opposition to this measure very largely on two points, first of all that it is unconstitutional and secondly that it is undesirable as interfering with trade and private affairs.
With regard to the constitutional aspect of the question, we had that matter discussed earlier in the evening from the purely legal standpoint. I do not profess to be an expert in legal matters but I do know enough of the history of law to recognize that it is very largely a history of changes in public opinion and the very slow and lagging process of gradual change in law made reluctantly in an effort to come up to the existing development of public opinion. The law lags far behind, and it is only under very great pressure that at last we have recorded in our codes the decisions arrived at by the great majority of our people. I quite agree with the bon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr Kennedy) when he states that there is no clear cut line between criminal and noncriminal acts. A few years ago it was not a crime to hold slaves. Many people of the most worthy classes held slaves, and justified themselves from the ethical standpoint in so doing. Undoubtedly in those days it was legal to hold slaves; there was no crime in it whatever. Then there arrived a time when it was declared to be a crime to hold slaves. I have not the slightest doubt that before that time there would be a great deal of legal argument to the effect that to do away with slavery would be an infringement upon the rights of private property. That would be a logical argument, because men had private property in the possession of slaves and, as the rights of private property were understood up to that time, the taking away of the slaves would be an infringement.
It seems to me that to-day we face the necessity of a higher code, a new code if you like, with regard to the protection of society, necessitated by the new conditions which have developed in this industrial period. To a certain extent competition used to act as a regulator. I am pleased that the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) pointed out that fact so clearly, but I believe he would also recognize that to a very large extent competition has ceased to be a regulator to-day.

I would suggest to the hon. member for Weyburn that he read the laws already on the statute books. In a debate only a few days ago on the marketing act the hon. member for Northumberland protested against producers being coerced, and against their being enforced to adopt ideas and policies tabulated or formulated in the minds of so-called supermen who have been chosen by the Minister of Agriculture to tell Canadians what the producers know better than he knows. The hon. member waxed eloquent when he was speaking about the matter, stating that the Natural Products Marketing Act was the most vicious piece of legislation ever placed on the statute books of Canada. He said it was impossible to prevent bootlegging in liquor and he wondered how we could prevent bootlegging in potatoes. He asked how an ordinary decent Canadian citizen such as he himself claimed to be could possibly be prevented from selling his goods in any way he pleased. He wanted to know what you could do with him if he refused to sell his apples, and so on and so on. In connection with one of the clauses I happen to have had my attention called to the Milk Control Act of 1934 of the province of Ontario, which was modified very slightly by the Liberal government this year in order to make it more stringent. Let us see what they are doing in the province of Ontario. I quote from the act:
The board shall have jurisdiction and power upon its own initiative, or uipon complaint or request made to it in writing, to inquire into any matter relating to the producing, supplying, processing, handling, distributing or sale of milk and, subject to the approval of the lieutenant governor, to make regulations with respect thereto or to any of the said matters.
I want to call this to the attention of the hon. member for Northumberland. As I have said, the act was under review by the Liberal government in Ontario this year which made one or two slight modifications to make it more drastic. Quoting from the act again:
(a) governing and supervising the producing, processing, handling, storing, hauling, delivering, distributing, keeping or offering for sale and the sale of milk, and all persons engaged or employed therein, and the reports and returns to be made by them to the board;
I suppose that what is true of milk may conceivably be true of potatoes or apples. I quote further from the act:

(a) requiring per sons or classes of persons engaged or employed in the processing, handling, storing, hauling, delivering, distributing, keeping or offering for sale, or the sale of milk to be licenced and to fix the term of such licences and the fetes to be paid therefor;
(c)	governing disputes and the determination of disputes arising between producers and distributors of milk, or between any two or more classes or branches of persons engaged in the milk industry as producers, processors, handlers, haulers, distributors or vendors of milk, or as being otherwise engaged in the said industry;
(d)	governing agreements which may be entered into between producers of milk and other persons or classes of persons engaged in the milk industry.
Surely that legislation is telling the producers what they have to do, and it provides for fines in connection therewith. I want to read one or two other brief sections to give the scope of the act:
No person shall engage or be employed in any branch of the milk industry as provided by and in accordance with this act and the regulations.
Again that is almost identical with the terms of the Natural Products Marketing Act, and certainly not less severe than that which we have before us this evening. Then section 11 :
Every person who violates any of the provisions of this act or of any regulation, rule or order made under this act or of the board shall incur a penalty of not less than $5 for each offence, recoverable under the Summary Convictions Act.
There you have a man made a criminal and fined for disobeying any of the regulations under the act.
That is what I objected to the other day.
Quite so, but I say that this is in force in the province of Ontario in regard to milk, and the whole act was under review and modified to make it more drastic by a Liberal government in Ontario.

I said
the other evening that I did not care whether it was a Liberal, Conservative or Cooperative Commonwealth Federation government. Two wrongs do not make a right.
My hon. friend repudiates the Liberal government of Ontario for retaining this law on the statutes?
No, the hon. member is away off the mark. I stated quite clearly what I had to say,

The province of
British Columbia under a Liberal government

Criminal Code Amendment
has taken very similar action. I am afraid the hon. member for Northumberland will have to withdraw himself from the Liberal party and its policies.

If I do I won't go down there among you; I can tell
you that.

That may be. I think the hon. member will have to adopt the policy of the ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) and form a party of his own. I repeat it was the Liberal government of Ontario that amended the Milk Control Act.
If I do form a party I will get further than you did in forming one.

I sent to the library a few minutes ago to try to obtain the official amendment that the Ontario government made to the Milk Control Act, but it was not available. I venture to read from the Canadian Co-operator of April, 1935, what I think may be taken as a correct copy of the amendment. This amendment to the Milk Control Act with respect to the prohibition of co-operative dividends, which was introduced by the Hon. Duncan Marshall, reads:
Notwithstanding anything in the Companies Act or in any letters patent of incorporation or supplementary letters patent or in any other general or special act contained, no person, firm or corporation shall give or distribute any fund, refund, rebate, interest or dividend to any purchaser of milk therefrom, either directly or indirectly in respect of such purchases of milk, except such interest or dividend as may be earned on capital invested by such purchaser in such firm or corporation.
And the Canadian Co-operator adds this note:
The exception in favour of payment of interest or dividends on their capital investment in dairies by milk consumers seems to be a deliberate discrimination in favour of capitalist dairies. In recnt years it has been the practice of some of them to conduct campaigns for the sale of dairy securities to producers and consumers of milk. Capitalist dairy corporations are specifically enabled to distribute their profits 'in a manner agreeable to them, but that right is denied to cooperative dairies.
I have read this amendment because I think there is a danger that we do precisely the same thing if we pass section 498A (1) without some modification or without adding some safeguarding clause. I received a letter the other day from the secretary of the Co-operative Union of Canada, who points out that:
While manifestly not intended to embarrass cooperatives or to obstruct the practice of
cooperative principles, it is possible that the distribution of the net profit surplus made by cooperative wholesales among retail societies might legally be construed to be within the prohibition of the payment of discounts, rebates or allowances, and a similar distribution of the net profit, surplus, by retail societies among consumers might legally be interpreted as reducing net prices to unreasonably low figures. The question of motive is a difficult one to establish in law, but unsympathetic courts might find as a fact that cooperative societies operate "for the purpose of destroying competition or eliminating a competitor."
He suggests that the following be added1 as an addendum to section 498A(1) of the criminal code, and I draw the minister's attention to this in order that perhaps he himself may see fit to incorporate it in the draft:
The provisions of this subsection shall not, however, prevent a cooperative society returning to producers or consumers, or a cooperative wholesale society returning to its constituent retail members, the whole or any part of the net surplus made in its trading operations in proportion to purchases made from or sales to the society.
It would seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that an amendment of that kind would safeguard the cooperative societies. From the present draft I do not think the government is intending to penalize the cooperative societies but since it may have that effect I believe something of this kind is highly desirable.
Mr. 'GUTHRIE: I may tell my hon. friend that a suggestion has been made already in the language in which he has moved it, and the view of the law officers is that this section as drawn would not apply to the cooperative societies. However, it may be necessary to clarify the matter and I will let my hon. friend know the next time the bill is before the house.

I thank the minister. I wanted this matter made very dear because while it is desirable to curb the avaricious practices indicated by the report of the price spreads commission, it is an altogether different thing for people to organize cooperatively and return their dividends. The report of the price spreads commission urges:
-further development of consumers' cooperatives in Canada would' be of general benefit.
It has also declared that the movement-
-should not be victimized in the early stages of its development by unfair competitive practices or price discrimination on the part of manufacturers and wholesalers.
I have very little more to say on the bill as a whole, but in the few minutes left to me I should like to refer again to section 5.
Criminal Code Amendment

Anyone who has been Connected in any way with the labour movement or who has been in close contact with industrial affairs must realize that in many cases the employee is almost helpless. We see this fact in its most exaggerated form in the company towns where a large corporation, very often an American corporation, practically controls the life of the whole community. It is quite obvious that in such cases the employee is helpless. It may be said that he can organize with others tout I submit that so far we have made no provision for the protection of the employee in his right to organize. Under these circumstances it has become practically impossible for employees to form a strong union. We in this house claim that this parliament is an impartial authority; as such it becomes incumbent upon us to protect the weaker members of society who are not in a position at the moment to protect themselves.
I cannot see why there should be such solicitude for the interests of the employers and 'the great corporations. Should an employee break a bit of machinery or smash a window he is considered a criminal, while through a Jong series of years employers have persisted in practices which have undermined the health of the workers, which have condemned them to a life in which they have no joy in living, and which have precluded them from the enjoyment of leisure. Yet these employers are not treated as criminals. In my judgment their crime is far more serious than that of the man who destroys a bit of property. Human life ought surely to be worth more than property. As yet we have hardly begun to protect human life, and while this legislation is far from being what I should like it to be, I feel that it is a gesture toward protecting the welfare of the employees and as such I welcome it.
Progress reported.
